label: October 2026
headline: October was narrow and oil-led: only 4 of 19 assets rose in rupees, and the regime reads Mixed, with credit and sector leadership turning defensive.
know: Markets turned cautious. Our market-mood gauge slipped from risk-on in September to mixed in October, and only 4 of 19 investments rose in rupees, half as many as the month before.
Oil is the big story. Fear of a wider Iran war pushed Brent crude up 17.7% in rupees in October and 41% over three months. It is the only risk asset that has led for three months running.

Interest rates are heading up, not down. Markets give a 94% chance that the US Fed raises rates on 9 December and 88% that the RBI does on 4 December, because inflation is above both central banks' targets.

sections.title: Regime: Mixed, leaning defensive
sections.body: Three of six votes were risk-on: copper/gold (+5.7% over 3 months), Midcap 150/FMCG (+2.6%) and equal-weight/cap-weight S&P 500 (+0.5%). Three were defensive: high yield/Treasuries (−1.8%), cyclical sectors lagging defensives (US −7.5pp, India −3.7pp over 3 months), and the US high-yield spread widening 0.59pp to 3.44%. Bonds & cash was the only family with a positive average return (+0.7%); global equity (−4.1%) and crypto (−8.2%) were weakest. Fed net liquidity fell 1.4% over 3 months to $5,746bn, and Global M2 growth slowed to +4.8% annualised over 3 months from +8.5% year on year.

sections.title: Persistence: one durable leader
sections.body: Brent crude is the only risk asset in the top 5 on both 1-month and 3-month returns, up 41.0% over 3 months. INR cash is the other persistent leader, which in a month when 15 of 19 assets fell reflects weakness elsewhere rather than strength. Emerging markets (−5.2% over 3 months) and silver (−15.2%) are persistent laggards. Leadership turned over: only 2 of September's top 5 stayed there, and the rank correlation with September was +0.09, so this month's order bore little relation to last month's. US long Treasuries and the Nifty 50 each climbed 13 places; Bitcoin fell 15 and the Nasdaq 100 fell 13.

sections.title: Divergences: credit and AI hardware
sections.body: Credit is weaker than equities: the high-yield spread widened 0.59pp over 3 months while the S&P 500 still returned +0.9% in rupees over the same period. AI hardware and Indian IT moved apart sharply: semiconductors (SMH) fell 15.0% in rupees while Nifty IT rose 18.1%, a 33.1pp gap. There was no liquidity divergence: global equities (−2.2% over 3 months) fell alongside Fed net liquidity and G3 central-bank assets. The VIX rose 3.1 points to 19.4, but equities fell too, so prices and fear agreed.

sections.title: Currency: a small headwind this month
sections.body: The rupee strengthened 0.9% in October (USD/INR 94.94), trimming rupee returns on dollar assets by about 0.9pp. Over 12 months the rupee has weakened 7.0%, which has added to the rupee return of every dollar asset over the year.

sections.title: Global markets: India led, Asian tech sold off
sections.body: In rupees, India was the best of 12 world equity markets in October (Nifty 50 +2.0%), though only 8th over three months (−5.3%). Asian technology markets fell hardest: Korea −17.1%, China tech −16.6% and Taiwan −11.3%, in step with the global semiconductor selloff. China markets averaged −9.7% against India's +2.0%, so October's foreign selling of India was not money rotating into China. Government bond yields fell in five of six major markets; only India's rose (+0.32pp), which widened its gap over the US to 2.25pp. Japan's 10-year yield is up 1.15pp over 12 months, but the yen showed no sign of stress. Against the rupee, the euro fell 2.5% in October; over 12 months the yuan gained 14.4% and the dollar 7.0%.

sections.title: Valuations: the US and Europe look expensive, India sits in the middle
sections.body: Against their own history, the most expensive markets are Taiwan (P/E 25.1, 96th percentile), Germany (18.2, 95th), the UK (17.1, 91st) and the S&P 500 (23.6, 85th). The cheapest are Korea (8.4, 9th) and Hong Kong (13.4, 10th). India's Nifty 50 sits in the middle: a P/E of 19.3 against a median of 19.3 (49th percentile since 2005), although its P/B of 2.83 is near the bottom of its history (6th percentile), so the reading depends on the measure. Midcaps (P/E 26.3, 22nd percentile of their history since 2021) sit below their median of 30.5, and small caps (31.3, 46th percentile) are close to theirs. Against bonds, shares look their least attractive in 20 years in the US, where the earnings yield is 0.90pp below the 10-year Treasury yield (1st percentile), and in Germany and the UK. Within India, Realty (3rd percentile), FMCG (11th) and Banks (12th) are the cheapest sectors against their own history and Pharma the most expensive (75th). Japan's P/E fell 23% in October on an earnings-data update rather than a market move, so treat its reading with care. Our backtest found that starting valuation alone did not reliably predict the next year's return for either the S&P 500 or the Nifty 50, so these readings are context for long-term weights rather than a timing signal.

sections.title: Risks: markets price a December Fed hike
sections.body: Prediction markets, as of 27 November, put a 25bp Fed hike in December at 94% (up from 76% thirty days earlier) and no Fed cuts this year at 98%. A 25bp RBI hike is priced at 88%, but that market is thin. The largest repricings were in Bitcoin, where the odds of falling to $55,000 at some point before year-end rose from 10% to 46% and of reaching $90,000 fell from 44% to 3%, and in gold, where the odds of falling to $3,500 by December rose from 11% to 62%. A US recession by year-end is priced at 3%; an AI bubble burst by June 2027 at 38% (up 16 points). Polymarket and Kalshi agree on all 6 outcomes checked. The VIX (19.4) and India VIX (15.3) are both up over 3 months. No asset is stretched on trend.

sections.title: Positioning: some bets lean against October's moves
sections.body: Leveraged funds are the most bullish on Nasdaq 100 futures in three years (94th percentile) even though the index fell 6.7% in October, so further selling could follow if they cut those positions. Asset managers hold their smallest Treasury bond long in three years (0th percentile) while bonds rallied 5.6%. Foreign investors sold a net ₹34,843 crore of Indian equities in October, yet the Nifty 50 rose 2.0%: domestic buyers carried the market. Hedge funds are the least long on silver in three years (3rd percentile). Looking ahead, options price a Nifty move of about ±3.5% by the 29 December expiry and ±4.9% for the S&P 500 by 18 December (as of 26–27 November).

sections.title: Breadth: a narrow month
sections.body: Only 4 of 19 assets rose in rupees and 3 beat INR cash (+0.45%): Brent (+17.7%), US long Treasuries (+4.7%) and the Nifty 50 (+2.0%). The gap from best to worst was 36.6pp, Brent to silver (−18.9%). Cross-asset dispersion was 7.1%, a little above its 12-month median of 6.4%.

questions: Credit spreads are widening and defensive sectors lead in both the US and India. Does our current risk level suit a Mixed regime?
Brent has led for three months (+41%). Is our energy and commodity exposure a deliberate position or drift?
Indian IT and global semiconductors moved 33 points apart in a month. Which side of the AI trade are we on, and through which holdings?
Markets price a December Fed hike at 94%. How exposed are our long-duration bonds and US holdings to a hike?
The rupee has weakened 7% over 12 months but strengthened in October. Should any of the dollar sleeve be hedged?
Domestic buyers absorbed ₹34,843 crore of foreign selling in October. How much do our Indian holdings depend on that domestic flow continuing?
Asian tech markets fell 11% to 17% in rupees in October. How much of our global equity sits in Korea, Taiwan and China tech, directly or through emerging-market funds?
The S&P 500, Germany, the UK and Taiwan are expensive against their own history while Korea and Hong Kong are cheap. How much of our global equity sits in each, directly or through broad funds?
